newsitem.title: UK: Brown says UK's Labour will be at heart of Europe.
newsitem.headline: Brown says UK's Labour will be at heart of Europe.

text.p: The opposition Labour party promised on Wednesday to play a leading role in Europe if it wins the election, warning that another Conservative victory would hurt Britain's interests.

In a high profile speech in New York, Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown said Eurosceptics opposed to links with Europe were driving policy in the ruling party, horrifying the business community and damaging investment and jobs.

"The Conservative party's drift towards isolationism which started as a trickle from the right of the party has now become a flood engulfing both left and right...," Brown said in a text distributed in London.
"Whether they admit it or not, for today's Tories (Conservatives) being pro-British has to mean anti-European...
"It is this school that has won the day in the Conservative party. The Conservatives now believe it possible for Britain to survive outside an integrated continent," Brown said.
But Brown told a meeting of the USA-EEC Association Britain could not afford to give up membership of the European Union.
"Our future lies in Europe, for good and obvious reasons. It is where we are, it is where we trade, it is where we find our prosperity and security," said Brown.
Brown is more pro-European than some Labour colleagues. But he is the dominant figure in his party's economic preparations with an election months away and Labour well ahead in the polls.
His intervention is likely to fuel an acrimonious row between Conservative Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke,
Rifkind, in Bonn for a speech on Britain's attitude to the European Union, told a BBC interviewer that on balance the government was hostile to a single currency.
Clarke, the most pro-European of Major's senior colleagues, said Rifkind had made "a slip of the tongue".
But Rifkind, just hours later, stood by his comment, delighting so-called Eurosceptics in the ruling party.

The row shattered an uneasy truce signalled last month when Rifkind and Clarke emerged from a cabinet meeting to declare that while Britain was keeping its options open, it was unlikely to join if the currency went ahead as planned in January 1999.
Brown studiously avoided mentioning the single currency in the remarks prepared for delivery in New York.
Labour has pledged to keep its options open on the single currency and to hold a referendum before joining, but has said it is unlikely a Labour government would join in 1999.
Brown said that business and investors were horrified at the rightward drift of the Conservatives on Europe.

"The vast majority of British companies and financial leaders would agree that continued EU membership is essential if we are to open Europe's markets. Leaving would horrify the business community," Brown said.
But he said Labour would press for changes in Europe to improve the business climate, including strengthening competition policy and improving job creation.
"We are hostile to the notion that a single currency can proceed at any stage on a non-convergent basis," they said in response to a Reuter query.
"Government policy has not changed," they added.
